title: How would you estimate how many office chairs UK employers buy each year?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many office chairs do UK employers buy each year?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: UK employers buy roughly 1.6 million office chairs a year: about 12M desk chairs in use, replaced every eight years or so, plus a little extra for new desks. The two things that change the answer most are hybrid working, which cuts the number of desks per worker, and how long a chair really lasts. Have a go yourself before reading on.
body:
The question

How many office chairs do UK employers buy each year?

This is a business-to-business estimate, so define who buys and what counts:

  • Which chairs? Desk (task) chairs only, or meeting-room and reception seating too? Default to desk chairs.
  • Which employers? Private companies, public sector offices and charities all count. Schools and hospitals buy different furniture, so leave them out.
  • Home offices? Chairs people buy for themselves are out. Chairs employers fund for home working are a grey area: exclude them from the main answer and treat them as an add-on.
"I'll estimate desk chairs bought by UK employers for their offices, and handle home-working chairs separately."

The approach: installed base ÷ lifespan, plus growth

Chairs are durable goods, so yearly purchases come from two sources:

  1. Replacement: chairs in use ÷ years a chair lasts.
  2. Growth: new desks as the office workforce grows.

The quick version, 15M desk workers ÷ 7 years = about 2.1M, assumes every desk worker has their own chair in an office. Since hybrid working became common, many offices have fewer desks than staff, so you need a step that converts workers into desks.

Step by step

  1. Desk workers: 15M. About 30M people are on UK payrolls and around 4M more are self-employed. Assume a bit under half of all workers do desk-based jobs: roughly 15M.
  2. Desks per desk worker: 0.8. With hybrid working, many offices share desks. Assume four desks for every five desk workers. 15M × 0.8 = 12M desk chairs in use.
  3. Replacement: 8-year life. A decent office chair lasts eight to ten years; cheaper ones less. 12M ÷ 8 = 1.5M chairs a year.
  4. Growth: 1% more desk workers a year. 15M × 1% = 150,000 new desk workers × 0.8 desks = 120,000 chairs.
Source of demandChairs a year
Replacement (12M ÷ 8)1,500,000
Growth (150,000 × 0.8)120,000
Total1,620,000

Answer: about 1.6M office chairs a year. Replacement is over 90% of it, so this is a mature, steady market.

Sanity check from a second angle

From one office. Picture a firm with 100 desk workers. At 0.8 desks each it has 80 chairs. Replacing them every eight years means about 10 new chairs a year, plus roughly one for growth. Eleven chairs a year for a 100-person office sounds like a realistic order for a facilities manager. Scale that up: 15M desk workers is 150,000 such offices, × 10.8 chairs = 1.62M.

By spend. At an average of $300 a chair, 1.62M chairs cost about $490M, or roughly $32 per desk worker a year. That is a small line in any office budget, which fits: chairs are cheap relative to rent and salaries.

Which assumption matters most?

ChangeNew total
Chair lasts 7 years, not 81.83M
Chair lasts 10 years, not 81.32M
0.6 desks per worker, not 0.81.25M

Plausible changes to lifespan or desk sharing move the answer by 10% to 25%. A one-off office refurbishment wave would add a temporary spike on top.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I estimate about 1.6 million chairs a year. That's 12 million desk chairs in use, 15 million desk workers with four desks for every five people, replaced every eight years, plus about 120,000 for growth. The swing factors are desk sharing and chair life: more desk sharing could take it down to about 1.25 million. For a furniture maker, it's a replacement market, so winning large framework contracts with big employers matters more than chasing new offices."

A weak answer divides 15M by 7 and stops, ignoring hybrid working and never asking whether the answer passes a common-sense test.

Common mistakes

  • Using all workers. Retail, construction and care workers do not sit at office desks. Start from desk-based workers.
  • One chair per worker. Desk sharing breaks that link. Convert workers to desks.
  • Mixing employer and personal purchases. Home chairs bought by employees are a separate consumer market.
  • Forgetting channel. A manufacturer sells through dealers, online and direct to big employers, at different prices per chair. Volume alone does not give revenue.

Practise it

1. One in five desk workers gets an employer-funded chair for home working, replaced every eight years. How many extra chairs a year?

Show the answer

15M × 20% = 3M home chairs ÷ 8 years = 375,000 chairs a year, which would lift the total to about 2M. This is why the home-office definition matters.

2. A manufacturer has 15% of unit volume at an average price of $250. What is its revenue from UK office chairs?

Show the answer

1.62M × 15% = 243,000 chairs × $250 = about $61M.

3. A big employer with 20,000 desk workers moves from 0.8 to 0.6 desks per worker. How many chairs does it stop needing?

Show the answer

Before: 20,000 × 0.8 = 16,000 chairs. After: 20,000 × 0.6 = 12,000. It frees 4,000 chairs, and its yearly replacement need falls from 2,000 to 1,500 at an eight-year life.

Where to practise next

For another replacement-cycle estimate, try car tyres sold in the UK or laptops bought by UK students. When to start from buyers or sellers is covered in which side to size a market from, and the market sizing drills give you timed practice.
